newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai B shares need better companies - brokers.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai B shares need better companies - brokers.

text.p: Brokers in Shanghai on Thursday called for more and better companies to be listed on the city's foreign currency B share market to help resolve the crisis as the index continues to fall.
They said an end to a ban on local investors trading B shares would also give a welcome short-term boost to the market, which has hit all-time closing lows on three days this week.
The B share index lost 0.165 points or 0.35 percent to end at a new low of 46.478 points on Thursday in slow trading, with most investors sidelined.

"The damn thing keeps on falling and there's no reason it's going to stop given the fact that there's so few companies on the Shanghai B share market that foreigners want to put money into," said one foreign brokerage analyst.
"The only way they can save it is to get some good companies out there," the analyst added.
"The simple answer is that the companies need to improve their performance," said another analyst.

Virtually all the B share companies reported very poor 1995 and 1996 half-yearly results and there are few brokers around who are optimistic on the prospects for a turn-around in the 1996 full-year results or even 1997.
Shanghai stock exchange officials said earlier this year that they planned to make development of the B share market a major part of its activities in 1996.

But the exchange has this year only listed five new B share companies, taking the total number of companies with foreign currency listed shares on the exchange to 41, far below the expectations and hopes of foreign brokers.
"What kind of a developing market is that?" asked another brokerage analyst. "Forty-odd shares and that's it? Is this where we say goodbye? It's a bit dull to be quite honest."
The B shares staged a minor rally in the middle of the year thanks to a sudden influx of money from local Chinese investors who are theoretically forbidden to buy B shares.
But the authorities then issued warnings which have largely scared locals away, thereby removing the only significant support for B share prices.
"It's a bit illogicial to keep locals out of the market at this point since they're the only people interested in putting money into it, but it's rather a short-term solution," the analyst added.

If the exchange wants to eventually become a stock market on the same level as Hong Kong or other major regional centres, they have to pay more attention to the number and quality of the companies that are listed, the analyst said.
"They have to address not just the liquidity problem, but also the fundamental problem of the market which keeps it unattractive to foreigners," she said.

"The attraction of the B shares for locals has nothing to do with the quality of the companies, it's only because of the relatively inexpensive P/E ratios compared with the (domestic) A shares," she added.
Analysts said the Chinese securities authorities were concentrating more at present on listings of major companies on the international markets such as Hong Kong, rather than Shanghai.
